author: jnack
content:
I have been reading back in here a bit and i must say it is depressing to read that criticism on keeping a decomp repo private is viewed as toxicity.

This server is full of public decomp repositories, so it is kind of a shock to see one being kept private, especially for a game as popular as sunshine, especially with how much progress it has.

I agree with encounter, that because of this private project, it makes sense to warn potential decompers for sunshine to essentially not bother doing the work twice.
And in the same breath, it also feels pretty short sighted and odd to actively refuse that collaboration, while being in this server that is heavily focused on collaboration.

No one can force the project to become public, but they have every right to critique the issue, as long as as mentioned, no one is taking those critiques further to actively harass/attack. Criticism in itself is not a bad thing.

I sincerely hope you reconsider your views here because it really doesnt feel beneficial to anyone to keep it private.

author: LocalH
content:
I think as part of a shared culture, the work done to understand these works of art in a much deeper sense than merely playing them should be somewhat public, in a philosophical sense. This *is* digital archaeology, in every sense of the word. You may be an amateur archaeologist who prefers to work alone and in private, and that is your prerogative, but at the same time others may not wish to attempt to also dig on the same site you're working on, because *they* may not wish to duplicate work that's already been done. And that is *their* prerogative as well. 

The analogy isn't perfect, of course, because digital things can be easily duplicated while physical things cannot. But the fact remains is that these works (the games themselves) will one day ultimately be fully public domain, by design. That's what makes them "shared culture". So I strongly believe that projects to decompile them into a form that will help ensure the works *survive* in such a form to become public domain one day, I think all such projects should at least be quasi-public. They don't necessarily have to be fully public, but there should be a way for someone to contribute and to see the direct progress of the decomp. Otherwise there's kind of a feeling (that I'm not assuming you have but this is my gut) that you make use of tooling but aren't giving anything "back" in a sense. That probably isn't your direct intention, I admit that fully. But nonetheless it's very easy to perceive that to be a possibility, and perception is a hell of a drug for all of us. 

As with jnack, I strongly and sincerely hope you reconsider your views, for the good of preservation and game development understanding.
